concept.name: Certificate of deposit
concept.definition: A time deposit with a specific maturity, traditionally evidenced by a certificate: the depositor commits a fixed amount for a fixed period — such as six months, one year, or five years — and in exchange the issuing bank or credit union pays a stated rate of interest. Large-denomination CDs are typically negotiable and can trade in secondary markets.
concept.intuition: A CD is a locked savings box: you lend the bank a fixed sum for a fixed term at a fixed rate, and you pay a penalty if you break the lock early.
concept.mechanics: Retail CDs pay interest to maturity, are typically FDIC-insured up to statutory limits, and impose early-withdrawal penalties. Callable CDs give the issuing bank — not the holder — the right to redeem early, usually exercised when rates fall; negotiable (jumbo) CDs trade among institutions like other money-market paper.
concept.failure_modes: Early withdrawal triggers penalties or forfeited interest; callable CDs are redeemed away precisely when reinvestment rates have fallen; balances above deposit-insurance limits are exposed to bank failure; and fixed rates lose purchasing power under inflation.
concept.misconceptions: That a 'one-year non-callable' CD matures in one year — the non-call period is how long the bank cannot redeem it, which can be much shorter than the actual maturity. Also, CDs and negotiable CDs differ: the latter trade and fluctuate in price.
concept.example: A saver places $10,000 in a one-year CD at 4.5% APY and receives $10,450 at maturity; withdrawing after six months would forfeit roughly three months of interest.
